body:
From the Jolt documentation:

> Note that the physics simulation works best if you use SI units (meters, radians, seconds, kg). In order for the simulation to be accurate, dynamic objects should be in the order [0.1, 10] meters long, have speeds in the order of [0, 500] m/s _**and have gravity in the order of [0, 10] m/s^2**_. Static object should be in the order [0.1, 2000] meter long. If you are using different units, consider scaling the objects before passing them on to the physics simulation.

What happens if you set the gravity too high is that the acceleration becomes so big that in 1 time step you can cover a lot of distance. By default bodies are updated in discrete time steps which means that they can end up quite far in the floor in a single time step. The simulation will push the object out in the next time steps, but as you say, you can see that happening. This is not limited to capsules, it will happen with any shape type.

You can increase the simulation frequency as you already tried or you can set the 'Continous CD' option on the rigid body to prevent the object from penetrating.

But with a gravity as high as this, you're bound to run into issues as the simulation has not been tweaked for this. E.g. restitution will most likely break.

Hi @jrouwe, thanks for the reply.

> What happens if you set the gravity too high is that the acceleration becomes so big that in 1 time step you can cover a lot of distance.

This is understandable. It is what I would expect for a high gravity.

However **with a default physics tick of 60, and a a default gravity of 9.8, capsule rigidbodies will also very visibly sink into the ground.** In fact, in the video I shared with you I showcase how the default gravity still reproduces this. 
The default 9.8 fits the ranges specified on the Jolt documentation snippet you've sent. 
Can be reproduced using my MRP as template for it. Just change the gravity to 9.8.

> You can increase the simulation frequency as you already tried or you can set the 'Continous CD' option on the rigid body to prevent the object from penetrating.

The issue (on 9.8 gravity) does improve a lot by setting the physics tick to 120, but my MRP and video really do show how easy it is to get capsule rigidbodies to sink into static bodies.

My report is so long precisely because there's a lot of nuances and tried workarounds to explain on this issue.

In any case, the key (implementation) issue is default gravity floatyness.

There's an actual objective to be achieved with Godot, that I simply cannot currently meet, which is **getting a faster fall velocity on capsule rigidbodies** without the sinking.

If I were to use a higher gravity to achieve this fall speed using Unity, I wouldn't be encountering the issues I'm encountering with Godot Jolt.

I may be forced to use a CharacterController3D, as for some reason, these don't seem to have the same problems, even using a capsule collision at a high gravity (although I must admit I haven't tested this, the video shared by _booch is quite clear, even though he might not have such a high gravity, yet his rigidbody does sink with ease compared to the charactercontroller). Why could that be?

I understand any technology has it's limitations which is why I'm very **open to workarounds, but achieving this faster fall speed is crucial**. I do prefer using a capsule based rigidbody though, it is how many people approach character controlling, and it's a great easy solution for slopes, cumulative forces and more dynamic physics in general. So what would you suggest? How would you implement this faster fall speed without bodies sinking?

As of writing this I am attempting to restructure my game's physics to a higher simulation frequency (240+!!) and CCD, without renouncing to a high gravity for fast falling (which is the most obvious and cleanest solution I can think of for that), but I fear since it affects all physics it may come at a substantial performance cost or even the drawbacks you mention.

If I take your MRP with its default gravity of 100 and change the capsule to have CCD: then it doesn't sink (visually and according to your TTY output). If I reduce the gravity to 9.8 then it does sink in the floor with CCD. This is because CCD doesn't activate in your test because it doesn't consider the object to be moving fast enough to teleport through the floor. You can configure the speed at which it starts doing CCD. If I change the 'Continuous CD Movement Threshold' setting to 0.25 then CCD kicks in in this particular example and the object doesn't sink through the floor: You may need to play around with the setting a bit to get the best results. Note that very low values can result in artifacts if your body is able to rotate (around a non symmetrical axis).

@jrouwe That's it! The movement threshold setting + CCD enabled fixes the sinking, thank you!

CCD is one of the first things I checked when I first encountered this issue because Unity also has it and it helped a lot there.

However it never worked for me on Godot with high gravity, I wrongly asumed it was just broken or that I didn't understand how it was meant to work (well aparently I didn't since I ignored any velocity threshold values being invonved).

The only thing I could maybe say at this point is that default Continuous CD Movement Threshold `0.75` is maybe too high, even for a default `9.8` gravity, considering capsule shapes are going to be common for rigidbodies, however the current default value certainly is a lenient optimization for most rigidbody shapes, so it doesn't matter much. 

I'll certainly be adjusting this value in quite a few games I've made where this issue is present.
